summary: Defines an SNMP MIB for watching print jobs. It covers monitoring job status and progress, learning resource needs before a job runs, tracking resource use during printing, and collecting accounting data afterward. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: It is a scoreboard for the printer queue. You can see which jobs wait, which are printing, and how much paper they used.

questions: what is the job monitoring mib
how to monitor print jobs with snmp
subtitle: An SNMP standard for tracking printer jobs, their status, and resource use.

tldr.problem: Print servers and printers need a standard way to report job status (waiting, printing, done), resource consumption (paper, toner), and errors so that users and operators can track print jobs and billing can work.
tldr.mechanism: An SNMP MIB (Management Information Base) defines tables for jobs, attributes, state, and resource tracking. Agents in printers or servers populate these tables as jobs arrive, progress, and complete. Monitoring applications query the tables via SNMP.
tldr.outcome: Operators can see which jobs are printing and why jobs are stuck. Users can check if their job finished and where it is. Accounting systems can track paper and toner use per job and per user.

today: RFC 2707 is informational and published by the Printer Working Group, not the IETF. The IESG notes that it represents an unconventional MIB design and does not endorse it as a model for future MIBs. However, it has been deployed in printers and print servers for job monitoring and accounting.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Job Monitoring MIB is a Printer Working Group standard published as an informational RFC. It defines SNMP objects for monitoring print jobs, from submission through completion and beyond. The MIB serves multiple roles: users track their own jobs, operators monitor all jobs in a queue and detect problems, and accountants collect resource-use data for billing.

The MIB was designed to work with many job submission protocols (IPP, ISO DPA, IEEE 1284.1) and to work with both simple printers and complex multi-device systems. It is not limited to printing; fax and scanning could be added later.

A key design principle: the agent SNMP software sits as close as possible to the job processing. This might be in the printer itself (Configuration 1), in a server that sends jobs to printers (Configuration 2), or split between server and printer (Configuration 3).
sections.eli5: The MIB is a rule book for how printers and servers report what is happening to each print job. SNMP is the network protocol used to read the information.

sections.title: Job Model and Terminology
sections.content:
The MIB uses precise terms from the ISO Document Printing Application (DPA) standard. A job is a unit of work whose results belong together, containing one or more documents. Each document is split into pages and printed on sheets. An impression is one pass of a sheet past the printer's marker (so a two-sided sheet is two impressions).

A job progresses through states: pending (submitted, waiting), processing (actively printing), processingStopped (paused or blocked), completed (done), canceled (user stopped it), or aborted (error stopped it). Each state can have state reasons—bits that explain why a job is in a state, such as 'printer is out of paper' or 'job is waiting for authentication.'

A job set is a group of jobs queued for a specific printer or set of printers. The MIB tracks oldest and newest active jobs in a job set so monitoring applications can quickly find active work without reading all completed jobs.
sections.eli5: A job is a thing you print. It sits in a queue with other jobs, and moves through states: waiting, printing, done. The MIB tracks which state each job is in.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Tables
sections.content:
The Job Monitoring MIB consists of four groups, each a table:

The General Group contains job-set-wide information: the number of active jobs, the index of the oldest and newest active jobs, and job retention time (how long completed jobs stay in the MIB for accounting).

The Job ID Group maps the job submission ID (the identifier that the client uses when submitting the job) to the internal jmJobIndex (the identifier the MIB agent uses). This mapping lets a monitoring application look up a specific job given the submission ID.

The Job Group contains one row per job with mandatory objects: job state (pending, processing, completed, etc.), state reasons (bits explaining why), owner, and processing progress (impressions completed, kilobytes processed).

The Attribute Group is the largest table, containing one row per job per attribute. Attributes specify job parameters (requested resources like paper type, finishing), job identification (owner, name, submit time), and job results (resources consumed, actual completion time). This separation (job table with mandatory fields, attribute table with optional ones) lets implementations support rich job data without requiring every field.
sections.eli5: The MIB is organized as several spreadsheets. One tracks active jobs, one maps submission IDs to internal IDs, one lists each job and its state, and one tracks details like paper used or finishing options.

sections.title: Job Attributes and Resource Tracking
sections.content:
Attributes are the heart of the Job Monitoring MIB. They represent job parameters, resource requests, and resource consumption as name-value pairs. Examples include:

Requested attributes: number of copies, finishings (stapling, folding), collation, paper type, print quality, two-sided printing, color mode.

Consumption attributes: kilobytes processed, impressions completed (sheets printed), estimated time to complete. These let users and operators see progress and operators predict when printers will be idle.

Resource accounting attributes: total pages printed, total sheets printed, media consumption (paper type and weight), toner/ink used, finishing operations performed. Accounting applications copy these values after a job completes to bill users or departments.

Each attribute has a type (integer or octet string) and enumerated values where applicable. Attributes are only present in the attribute table when they have a value; an attribute NEED NOT be present for every job. This sparse representation keeps the MIB table smaller and lets implementations choose which attributes to support.
sections.eli5: Attributes are details: 'this job needs 100 copies,' 'it used 50 sheets of paper,' 'it took 2 minutes to print.' The server tracks these so users and billing systems know what happened.

sections.title: System Configurations
sections.content:
The MIB supports three deployment configurations:

Configuration 1 (printer-centric): Clients submit jobs directly to a printer, and the printer itself contains the SNMP agent. Monitoring applications query the printer directly. This is simple for small networks but puts complexity in the printer.

Configuration 2 (server-centric): Clients submit jobs to a server (a print spooler or supervisor), which sends them to printers. The server contains the SNMP agent and reports on both jobs in the server queue and jobs in the printers. The printer does not have an agent. This concentrates management in the server but requires the server to know what is happening in each printer (obtained through non-SNMP means like device drivers).

Configuration 3 (split): Clients submit to a server, but the server does not have an agent. The monitoring application queries the printer's agent (after the printer receives the job from the server). The server may provide non-SNMP monitoring. This splits the load between server and printer agents but requires applications to monitor two sources.

Each configuration serves different deployment styles (single printers, printer pools, high-volume print centers).
sections.eli5: Three ways to set things up. The agent (the SNMP scoreboard keeper) can live in the printer, in the server, or split between both, depending on the system's size and design.

sections.title: Monitoring Applications and Use Cases
sections.content:
The MIB is designed for three main types of monitoring applications:

Single-job tracking: A user submits a job and monitors it. The application uses the job submission ID from the Job ID Group to find the job's row in the Job Group and Attribute Group, then polls for progress and completion.

Queue monitoring: An operator monitors all active jobs in a print queue, using the oldest and newest active job indexes to quickly find the active work. The operator can see job owners, progress, and state reasons (e.g., 'waiting for jam clearance') without reading completed jobs.

Accounting and usage collection: An accounting application periodically polls the MIB, records completed jobs' consumption attributes (pages, sheets, toner) to a database, and keeps a shadow copy of the attribute table for analysis and billing. The MIB's job persistence setting (how long completed jobs stay in the table) ensures the accounting application has time to copy the data.
sections.eli5: Three ways to use the scoreboard: check on your own job, see what is in the queue, or collect data for billing.
